findings.title: The single biggest programmatic SEO surface (city x category) ships with no canonical or hreflang
findings.principle: Every generateMetadata implementation for a locale-routed page must call buildAlternates (or an equivalent that emits canonical + all four language alternates + x-default) before the page is considered SEO-complete. A page listed in app/sitemap.ts is not allowed to ship without it.
findings.why: Without hreflang, Google treats /de/basel/coiffeur, /en/basel/coiffeur, /fr/basel/coiffeur and /it/basel/coiffeur as four separate pages with near-identical structure and only the category label translated, which is the textbook duplicate/thin-content pattern on a 4-language site. Google will pick one as canonical (usually arbitrarily) and the other three will be suppressed from the index or compete against each other, which is the opposite of what a city x category page exists to do (rank for local searches in each language market).
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/[city]/[category]/page.tsx generateMetadata (lines 44-77) returns only {title, description}; it never imports or calls buildAlternates. Contrast with app/[locale]/[city]/page.tsx line 45 (`const alternates = buildAlternates(city, locale);`) and app/[locale]/search/page.tsx which both do it correctly. app/sitemap.ts lines 113-124 emits this exact route for 6 cities x 4 categories x 4 locales, so 96 live URLs (24 unique page identities x 4 locale variants) carry zero canonical/hreflang signal.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "alternates\|buildAlternates" "app/[locale]/[city]/[category]/page.tsx" returned nothing. grep -rln "alternates" app/ listed [city]/page.tsx, search/page.tsx, salon/[slug]/layout.tsx and others but not [city]/[category]/page.tsx. grep -ri hreflang across _backend-system _docs _rules _design-system CLAUDE.md returned only a prior verification note about /de/basel, not the category page.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: lib/seo.ts's buildAlternates() is the correct, already-built helper and is correctly wired on [city]/page.tsx, search/page.tsx and salon/[slug]/layout.tsx. The delta is exactly one call site missing on the highest-volume programmatic page.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system has no SEO topic; this belongs in a new short SEO law file (e.g. _docs/SEO.md or a section of CLAUDE.md's design contract) stating the buildAlternates-on-every-sitemap-page rule.
findings.enforcement: gate: a PreToolUse or CI check that reads app/sitemap.ts's route list and greps each corresponding page.tsx for `buildAlternates` or `alternates:`; fails the build if a sitemap-listed dynamic route's generateMetadata has no alternates object.

findings.title: Category FAQ schema and city x category FAQ copy are hardcoded German and served under all four locale URLs
findings.principle: Any JSON-LD or visible copy embedded on a locale-routed page must branch on the resolved locale; hardcoding one language's text into structured data or an FAQ block on a route reachable at /en/, /fr/, /it/ is a hreflang-language mismatch and is never acceptable, even when the rest of the page is translated.
findings.why: Google's hreflang validation checks that the declared language of a URL (via lang attribute and hreflang tag) roughly matches the actual textual content; FAQPage schema in German embedded on a page whose hreflang claims fr or it is a mismatch signal that can cause Search Console hreflang warnings and can make Google distrust the whole hreflang cluster for that URL group, not just the one field.
findings.local_evidence: lib/seo.ts CATEGORY_FAQS (lines 48-71) is a single Record<string, FaqItem[]> with every question/answer written in German and every answer hardcoding "in Basel" (e.g. "Ein Haarschnitt bei einem Coiffeur in Basel kostet..."), imported and rendered via generateFaqSchema(CATEGORY_FAQS.coiffeur) with no locale parameter in app/[locale]/coiffeur/page.tsx, nails/page.tsx, spa/page.tsx and barbershop/page.tsx (all four, confirmed by grep). Separately, CityCategoryFaq() in app/[locale]/[city]/[category]/page.tsx (lines 79-119) renders hardcoded German h2 ("Häufig gestellte Fragen") and question text regardless of the `locale` variable already in scope, even though cityName and categoryName are correctly localized two lines above it.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "locale" lib/seo.ts around generateFaqSchema/CATEGORY_FAQS shows no locale parameter on either. grep -n "CATEGORY_FAQS" app lib shows the same four German-only import sites for /coiffeur, /nails, /spa, /barbershop with no per-locale variant selected. grep -ri hreflang across the law-layer directories returned nothing that would have caught this because the gap is content-language, not the alternates tag itself.
findings.existing_coverage: none: every other translatable string on these same pages (titles, descriptions per lib/seo.ts's own pattern used elsewhere, and the city/category names in the same file) IS correctly localized, so the pattern to follow already exists in the same file, it just was not applied to the FAQ block.
findings.where_it_should_live: the same new SEO law doc as finding 01, plus a note in CLAUDE.md's copy-economy section since this is also a copy-quality issue, not only technical SEO.
findings.enforcement: checklist item on any new customer-facing page: "every hardcoded string inside a generateMetadata/JSON-LD/FAQ block has a de/en/fr/it branch"; a lint rule flagging a bare German word list (Basel, Häufig, kostet) inside app/[locale]/** outside a de-locale conditional would catch regressions cheaply given the existing pattern already used for titles/descriptions.

findings.title: Salon structured data (JSON-LD LocalBusiness) hardcodes addressLocality to Basel for every salon in every city
findings.principle: Any field written into schema.org structured data must be derived from the entity's own data, never a hardcoded literal, even when the literal happens to be correct for a majority of current rows; a city/locality field on a LocalBusiness schema must resolve from the salon's actual address/postal code the same way the page's own visible copy does.
findings.why: Google uses LocalBusiness address data (via Merchant/local pack signals) to match a business to local search intent; a Zurich salon whose JSON-LD claims addressLocality: Basel is factually wrong data fed directly to Google's knowledge graph, which can misassign the salon to the wrong local pack, and it is also a fabricated-data violation under this project's own no-fabrication rule (taste rule 1) applied to machine-readable data instead of visible UI.
findings.local_evidence: lib/seo.ts generateSalonSchema() (line 193) sets `addressLocality: "Basel"` unconditionally for every salon passed in, with no read of salon.city_slug or salon.city_name (both of which exist on the Salon type, lib/types.ts lines 373-374, and are already used correctly nearby: app/[locale]/salon/[slug]/layout.tsx line 48 derives `const city = salon.postal_code ? postalToCity(salon.postal_code) : null;` for the same salon's title/description on the same page). app/sitemap.ts's own CITIES list (basel, zurich, bern, luzern, winterthur, st-gallen) confirms 5 of 6 live cities are not Basel, so this schema field is wrong for the majority of salons outside Basel.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "addressLocality" app lib returned exactly one hit, the hardcoded literal in lib/seo.ts:193. grep -ri "addressLocality\|structured data" _backend-system _docs _rules _design-system returned nothing, confirming no existing law addresses structured-data field correctness at all.
findings.existing_coverage: none, but a correct pattern to copy (postalToCity) already exists three files away in the same page's own layout.tsx.
findings.where_it_should_live: the SEO law doc; also worth a one-line note in _docs/BACKEND.md's data-modeling section since it is really a data-integrity bug wearing an SEO hat.
findings.enforcement: S1-style unit assertion: generateSalonSchema(salon) for a fixture salon with a non-Basel postal code must not return addressLocality === 'Basel'.

findings.title: Legally and financially significant transactional emails accept a locale argument and silently ignore it, always sending German
findings.principle: A template function's signature must not lie: if a function accepts a `locale: EmailLocale` parameter, its subject and body must branch on that parameter in every code path; a template with a locale parameter that has no effect on output is worse than one with no parameter at all, because every caller reasonably assumes localization is happening.
findings.why: A no-show charge, a late-cancellation fee, a refund, an upcharge, or an account suspension are financially or legally consequential notices; sending them only in German to a customer whose stored profile.locale is fr, it or en means that customer cannot understand why they were charged or suspended, which is both a support-ticket generator and, for the fee/charge emails specifically, arguably inadequate notice for a contested charge.
findings.local_evidence: lib/email-templates/audit-notifications.ts defines 19 functions (bookingPendingApprovalEmail through salonStrikeEmail, lines 3-147), every one typed `locale: EmailLocale = "de"` in its signature, and every one's subject/html string is hardcoded German with zero reference to the `locale` variable anywhere in the function body (confirmed by reading all 148 lines; `de=0 en=0 fr=0 it=0` locale-branch markers found by grep, versus lib/email.ts's 55-61 per-language markers in the properly localized templates). This is not dead code: lib/bookings/notify-no-show-fee.ts line 73 and lib/bookings/notify-refund.ts line 80 both correctly fetch `profile.locale` from the database and pass the real user locale into noShowChargeEmail/refundProcessedEmail, so a French-speaking customer's actual locale is threaded all the way to the template call and then dropped on the floor inside the template itself.
findings.absence_proof: grep -c 'de:' vs 'it:' etc across lib/email-templates/audit-notifications.ts returned 0/0/0/0, versus 8/8/8/8 for booking-notifications.ts and 10/10/10/10 for salon-onboarding.ts in the same directory, proving the other template files in the identical pattern DO branch and this one file does not. grep -rn for callers confirmed real invocation with a real per-user locale, ruling out the dead-code explanation.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the EmailLocale type, the per-locale label pattern (see lib/email.ts's `PL` object), and the caller-side locale resolution (profile.locale fallback to 'de') are all already correctly built; the only missing piece is that these 19 specific template bodies never use them.
findings.where_it_should_live: a comms law doc (new) stating the locale-parameter-must-branch rule, cross-referenced from lib/email-templates/README or a comment block at the top of lib/email.ts.
findings.enforcement: gate: a script that statically checks every exported function in lib/email-templates/**/*.ts and lib/email.ts whose signature includes `locale: EmailLocale`, confirms the function body contains at least 3 distinct locale-keyed branches (de/en/fr/it) in its subject or html; fails on audit-notifications.ts today, which is the correct behavior for a newly-added gate.

findings.title: The customer-facing email/SMS notification toggle is a complete silent no-op: no send path anywhere reads it
findings.principle: Any user-facing preference control that claims to change system behavior (a toggle, a checkbox, a settings row) must be read by every code path whose behavior it claims to govern, in the same commit that adds the control; a preference column that is written but never read is a promise the product breaks on every use.
findings.why: This is this project's own documented number-one failure mode (silent no-ops, named explicitly in CLAUDE.md's dedicated section) applied to comms: a user who switches off 'Email notifications' in Profile > Settings > Notifications reasonably believes solen.ch will stop emailing them, and nothing in the system honors that belief; if this ships as-is it is a broken promise the moment there is a real user to break it for, and depending on jurisdiction it can also be a consent-law problem (Swiss nFADP / GDPR-adjacent expectations both treat a displayed preference control as an enforceable commitment, not decoration).
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/profile/settings/notifications/page.tsx (and settings/SettingsForm.tsx) read and write `profiles.notification_email` / `profiles.notification_sms` via Supabase and render them as Switch components (SettingsForm.tsx lines 390-394, 479-483). A repo-wide grep for these two column names outside the settings/profile/type-definition files returns zero results: no cron job, no app/api/bookings/route.ts, no lib/email.ts, no lib/sms.ts call site reads either column before sending anything.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn "notification_email\|notification_sms" . --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx" --include="*.sql" across the whole repo (not just app/lib) returned only settings pages, SettingsForm.tsx, lib/types.ts, lib/database.types.ts and lib/validations.ts, 27 lines total, all read/write-for-display, zero read-before-send.
findings.existing_coverage: none for these two specific columns. A related but separate table, notification_preferences (deals_enabled, rebooking_enabled), IS correctly checked by welcome-series, rebooking-nudge and nail-infill-reminders (confirmed by grep on those three cron routes), so the pattern of honoring a preference exists elsewhere in the codebase, just not for this column pair.
findings.where_it_should_live: _docs/BACKEND.md already documents notification_preferences' two columns and explicitly calls out that review-prompt, birthday-messages, nail-infill and SMS reminders check no user-level preference (this is corroborating, independent confirmation from the descriptive doc); the missing piece is a LAW-layer rule, not a docs update.
findings.enforcement: gate: before merging any change that adds a sendEmail/sendSMS call, a check greps for at least one preference-column read in the same function or its call chain; short of that, a manual pre-launch checklist item is the minimum bar.

findings.title: No system-wide rule distinguishes transactional from marketing/nudge sends, so consent-checking is inconsistent across near-identical cron jobs
findings.principle: Every automated send must be classified at write-time as TRANSACTIONAL (always sends, tied to a specific booking/payment event the user directly triggered) or MARKETING/NUDGE (must check an opt-out/consent column before sending); the classification and its required check are declared once per cron job, not left to each job's author to decide ad hoc.
findings.why: Right now three nudge-style crons (welcome-series, rebooking-nudge, nail-infill-reminders) check notification_preferences and three others that are equally nudge/marketing in character (birthday-messages, review-prompt, daily-digest) check nothing at all; without a written rule for which bucket a new cron falls into, this split is accidental, not a decision, and the next cron someone adds has a coin-flip chance of being wired correctly.
findings.local_evidence: grep across all 25 app/api/cron/*/route.ts files for deals_enabled/rebooking_enabled/notification_email/notification_sms found hits only in welcome-series, rebooking-nudge and nail-infill-reminders; birthday-messages/route.ts (read in full, lines 1-30+) sends an unconditional email via lib/email.ts's sendEmail with no preference read anywhere in the file, and the same is true for review-prompt and daily-digest by the same grep.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn "deals_enabled\|rebooking_enabled\|notification_email\|notification_sms" app/api/cron/*/route.ts listed only 3 of 25 cron files; grep -ri "transactional\|marketing" across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, _design-system, CLAUDE.md returned only the one-line comment "Send a transactional email via Resend" atop lib/email.ts's sendEmail function, which documents the sending mechanism, not a classification rule for which templates require a consent check.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the notification_preferences table and its two columns already exist and are already the mechanism three jobs use; the missing piece is a declared rule for the other 22 jobs, most of which are legitimately transactional (booking confirmations, no-show fees) and correctly need no check, but a few (birthday-messages in particular, arguably review-prompt) are promotional in character and currently unchecked.
findings.where_it_should_live: a comms law doc; a short table naming all 25 cron jobs as TRANSACTIONAL or MARKETING with the required check is the concrete deliverable.
findings.enforcement: checklist: new cron PRs must state their classification in a comment at the top of the route file, matching the pattern _docs/BACKEND.md already uses to describe notification_preferences; a lint rule cannot easily infer intent here, so this stays a reviewed checklist item, not a hard gate.

findings.title: Every outbound email is HTML-only; Resend is never sent a plain-text alternative
findings.principle: Every transactional email payload sent to Resend must include both `html` and a derived `text` field (a stripped or hand-written plain-text version); an HTML-only multipart message is a spam-score and accessibility regression this project should not carry from day one.
findings.why: A missing text/plain MIME part is a well-known deliverability signal spam filters weight negatively (single-part HTML-only mail is disproportionately represented in spam corpora), and it breaks plain-text mail clients and some screen-reader/accessibility tooling; fixing this after volume ramps means re-touching every one of ~60 already-written templates instead of building the one shared sendEmail() wrapper correctly once.
findings.local_evidence: lib/email.ts's EmailPayload interface (lines 18-22) declares only `to`, `subject`, `html`; sendEmail() (lines 28-51) builds the Resend request body from exactly those three fields with no `text` key anywhere in the JSON.stringify payload. This is the single shared send function used by all ~60 template functions across lib/email.ts and lib/email-templates/*.ts, so the gap is systemic, not per-template.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "text:" lib/email.ts returned nothing. grep -ri "plain.text alternative\|plain-text email\|multipart" across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, _design-system, CLAUDE.md and both hook directories returned nothing, confirming this is entirely unaddressed anywhere in the law estate.
findings.where_it_should_live: the comms law doc; the fix is centralized in lib/email.ts's sendEmail() (one function), not per-template, since EmailPayload is the shared contract.
findings.enforcement: gate: a type-level check making `text` a required (not optional) field on EmailPayload would force every existing call site to supply one, which is the cheapest possible enforcement given TypeScript is already in the stack.

findings.title: A live outbound email cites a Swiss data-protection legal basis for sending without consent and links to an unsubscribe URL that does not exist
findings.principle: Any email whose footer promises an opt-out mechanism (a legal requirement for any send that is not strictly transactional) must link to a route that actually exists and actually suppresses future sends to that address; a dead unsubscribe link on a compliance-justified email is worse than no unsubscribe link, because it converts a good-faith legal defense into evidence the defense was never operational.
findings.why: salonOutreachInvitation is a cold outreach email sent to salon owners who have not opted in (their salon is merely listed), and its own footer text explicitly invokes 'nDSG Art. 31' as the legal basis for sending without prior consent, which under Swiss data protection practice is conditional on the recipient having a working, honored right to object; a 404 on the promised link removes that condition.
findings.local_evidence: lib/email.ts, function salonOutreachInvitation (lines 361-386), footer line 382: `Abmelden` followed by "Diese E-Mail wurde an ${to} gesendet, da Ihr Salon öffentlich gelistet ist (nDSG Art. 31)." No /unsubscribe route exists anywhere in the app directory (`find app -ipath "*unsubscribe*"` returns nothing), and no app/api endpoint handles an unsubscribe token or email parameter.
findings.absence_proof: grep -c "unsubscribe" lib/email.ts returned 1 (this single occurrence). find app -ipath "*unsubscribe*" returned zero files. grep -rn "unsubscribe" app/api returned nothing.
findings.existing_coverage: none; this is the only place in the codebase an unsubscribe promise is made at all, and it is unbacked.
findings.where_it_should_live: the comms law doc, plus this is urgent enough to also be a standalone _tasks/INCOMPLETE_FEATURES.md entry per the project's own incomplete-features convention.
findings.enforcement: gate: a simple route-existence check (does app/[locale]/unsubscribe or app/api/unsubscribe exist) run whenever lib/email.ts contains the literal string "/unsubscribe"; until then, treat this as a build-blocking TODO for any salon-outreach send at real volume.

findings.title: Booking confirmation, the single highest-volume transactional message, contains no actionable follow-through: no address, no map, no cancellation link, no calendar file
findings.principle: A booking confirmation message must contain, at minimum: the salon's address (or a map link), a link to view/manage/cancel the booking, and a way to add the appointment to the recipient's calendar (an .ics attachment or a one-click add-to-calendar link); a confirmation that only restates what the user just entered on the booking form is not doing the job of a confirmation.
findings.why: The entire value of a transactional confirmation over just closing the booking flow is that it survives independently of the session: the customer opens it later, often on a different device, to remember where to go and when, and to cancel if plans change; without an address/map or a cancel link, the email forces every one of those follow-up actions back into logging into the app and finding the booking manually, which is friction this project explicitly tries to eliminate everywhere else (per the booking-flow-canonical memory and the psychology system's guest-first law).
findings.local_evidence:
lib/email.ts function bookingConfirmation (lines 59-108): the `bodies` record for all four locales (lines 96-101) contains only `

Hello,

${service} at ${salon} on ${date} at ${time} is confirmed. See you there!

${priceHtml}

solen.ch

` (English shown, same shape in de/fr/it). No address field, no map link, no booking-detail/manage URL, no .ics attachment or add-to-calendar link anywhere in the function.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rli "\.ics\|icalendar\|VCALENDAR" lib app returned nothing repo-wide, confirming no calendar-file generation exists anywhere, not just in this template. Reading the full function body (lines 59-108) confirms no address/map/manage-link field is interpolated.
findings.existing_coverage: none in the email itself; the underlying data (salon address, booking id for a manage link) is already available to the caller (app/api/bookings/route.ts constructs the email with `booking.id` in scope for the error-reporting call two lines below), so this is a template-completeness gap, not a missing-data gap.
findings.where_it_should_live: the comms law doc's message-content-floor section; concretely, extend EmailPayload's vars for bookingConfirmation to accept `address`, `manageUrl`, and a generated .ics attachment.
findings.enforcement: checklist: a booking-confirmation-specific content floor (the four items named above) checked whenever this template is touched; not easily gate-able since it is a content-completeness judgment, not a structural pattern.

findings.title: No bounce, complaint, or suppression handling exists for outbound email; nothing stops re-sending to a dead or complaining address
findings.principle: Once real send volume exists, a webhook from the email provider (Resend) must record bounce and complaint events into a suppression table, and sendEmail must check that table before every send; until that volume exists, this is correctly deferred, not correctly absent forever.
findings.why: Repeated sends to a hard-bouncing or complaining address are the primary mechanism by which a sending domain's reputation degrades at providers like Gmail and Outlook; once reputation degrades, transactional mail (booking confirmations, payment receipts) starts landing in spam for everyone, not just the bad addresses, which is a much worse failure than the missing feature itself.
findings.local_evidence: find app/api -ipath "*resend*" -o -ipath "*webhook*email*" returned only app/api/bookings/resend-access (an unrelated booking-access-link resend feature, not an email-provider webhook). find app/api -ipath "*webhook*" shows only app/api/stripe/webhook/* ; there is no Resend webhook endpoint anywhere. grep -rli "bounce\|complaint" lib app returned no email/SMS-deliverability hits (only unrelated hits like booking dispute/report routes).
findings.absence_proof: find app/api -ipath "*webhook*" listed only Stripe webhook files. grep -ri "bounce\|sender reputation\|deliverability" across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, _design-system, CLAUDE.md returned nothing.
findings.where_it_should_live: the comms law doc, explicitly framed with a trigger, not as an immediate build item.
findings.enforcement: doc-only until the trigger fires; the trigger is concrete: once Solen sends more than roughly 500 transactional emails/day (the free Resend webhook capability makes this cheap even below that; the volume threshold is about when NOT having it starts costing sender reputation, roughly the point where a handful of stale/typo addresses recur across enough sends to matter statistically) or once any single salon/customer segment triggers a marketing-style send (birthday, rebooking nudge) at more than a few hundred recipients per run, wire the Resend webhook and a suppression table before that job goes live at that volume. At today's ~28 salons and pre-launch test data, building this now would be premature machinery per the project's own scale-discipline rule.

findings.title: SMS/email reminder timing (23.5-24.5h, presumably similar for 1h) is a single hardcoded global window, not a per-salon or per-category configurable policy
findings.principle: A reminder window may stay a single hardcoded constant while there is one plausible correct value for the whole marketplace; the moment two salon categories or two salons demonstrably want different reminder cadences (e.g. a spa wanting a 48h reminder because rescheduling a 90-minute treatment needs more notice, versus a barbershop wanting only 2h because walk-in-adjacent bookings are same-day), the window becomes a per-salon settings column, not a code constant.
findings.why: This is explicitly a scale-discipline call, not a criticism of the current value: a configurable reminder window is genuinely premature machinery for 28 salons with no evidence any of them want a different cadence, and building a settings UI for it now would be exactly the kind of big-company-first machinery this project's own doctrine warns against adopting early.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/cron/sms-reminders/route.ts lines 19, 42-44: `const win24hStart = new Date(now + 23.5 * 60 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();` and the matching win24hEnd, both literal numeric constants in the route file, not read from any salons.* column (the existing sms_reminder_24h/sms_reminder_1h columns are booleans, on/off, not the timing itself).
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "23.5\|24.5\|hours\|HOUR\|window" app/api/cron/sms-reminders/route.ts confirmed the literals; grep -rli "quiet.hour\|quiet_hour" lib app returned only an unrelated hit in app/api/slots/[id]/route.ts, confirming no reminder-timing configurability exists anywhere.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: whether to send at all is already a per-salon toggle (sms_reminder_24h/sms_reminder_1h); only the when is hardcoded.
findings.where_it_should_live: not a law-layer entry today; a QUESTIONS.md-style parked note is the right weight, naming the trigger explicitly: a salon owner or category (spa/nails with longer service times) asks for a different window, or booking-cancellation-due-to-late-reminder complaints appear in support data.
findings.enforcement: doc-only note, no gate warranted at this scale.

findings.title: Bare-path locale redirect uses Accept-Language + cookie with no documented, stable default-locale policy for crawlers
findings.principle: The locale a crawler or first-time visitor with no cookie is redirected to from a bare path (e.g. solen.ch/salon/foo) must be a single, documented, stable default (this project's default is 'de' per i18n.ts), and that default must be what x-default in hreflang alternates points to; Accept-Language-based redirects are acceptable for human visitors but must never be the value search engines see, since crawler Accept-Language behavior is inconsistent and unversioned by Google itself.
findings.why: If Googlebot's crawl requests (which may or may not send a consistent Accept-Language) get redirected to different locale variants across crawl sessions, Google can end up crawling and indexing inconsistent canonical targets for the same bare URL over time, which dilutes the ranking signal that would otherwise consolidate onto one clear canonical (the x-default target).
findings.local_evidence: middleware.ts getLocaleFromRequest (lines 6-32) resolves in order: URL path, then NEXT_LOCALE cookie, then Accept-Language header, then defaultLocale; the redirect (lines 80-85) is issued via NextResponse.redirect(url) with Next's default 307 status, not an explicit 301, for every bare path. lib/seo.ts buildAlternates() (lines 74-83) does correctly point x-default at /de, so the two pieces are not contradictory today, but nothing enforces that a locale-redirect change in middleware.ts stays in sync with the x-default choice in lib/seo.ts, since they are two unrelated files with no shared constant.
findings.absence_proof: grep -ri hreflang across the law-layer directories found no rule connecting middleware default-locale behavior to the x-default alternates value; the two files (middleware.ts's defaultLocale import from ./i18n, and lib/seo.ts's own hardcoded `de` in x-default) are not sourced from one shared constant, confirmed by reading both files directly.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the current values happen to agree (both effectively default to de); there is no test or gate that would catch them drifting apart.
findings.where_it_should_live: the SEO law doc, as a one-line invariant: x-default in buildAlternates must equal i18n.ts's defaultLocale, sourced from the same constant.
findings.enforcement: gate: lib/seo.ts should import defaultLocale from ./i18n instead of hardcoding "de" in two places (BASE_URL block and the x-default line), which turns this from a documentation rule into a structural impossibility to drift.
